newsitem.title: FRANCE: D.Bank economist urges German, French EMU action.
newsitem.headline: D.Bank economist urges German, French EMU action.

text.p: Germany and France must act soon to meet criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Deutsche Bank chief economist Norbert Walter said on Wednesday.
In a speech to a fund management conference, he said it was two-thirds likely that EMU would go ahead, and on time.
He said the greatest risk to the process was the possibility that France or Germany would fail to meet entry criteria.
"EMU without France doesn't come into existence. It is equally obvious that EMU without Germany doesn't come into existence," he said.
"The markets would ridicule a solution and it would not happen."

He said French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's election promises made it more difficult to achieve convergence criteria, and he faced possible opposition from the conservatives or even the communists in his coalition if he did take steps to achieve targets.
He said the French were wrong if they believed that the fiscal criteria were not taken that seriously.
"This was wrong and is wrong and therefore we are in trouble. The French don't believe the Germans are strict and thus act accordingly.
"Therefore France may be one obstacle to achieving the monetary union."
Walter also said Germany's second chamber of parliament, dominated by left wing parties would have to pass any piece of economic legislation, making it diffcult for Germany to achieve the criteria.
There was also the possibilty that certain indicators might not come out at the levels expected.
"We don't know whether the tax revenues will fall short of expectations or whether unemployment will surprise on the high side again."
Time was also running out for the government to take any fiscal decision that would have any bearing on the convergence criteria.

"Are we then hoping for luck to make it or should there be immediate action over the next few days. The government will have to have a decision by July 11. Watch out -- there are important decisions," he said.
Walter said the French had to act soon if they were to reach the criteria.
"The French believe that they could go on vacation in August and come back and make decisions thereafter. It is nonsense, they have to skip vacation this year."
Other countries due to be included in the first wave of EMU also had problems that needed to be resolved, he said, especially Finland, Portugal and Spain.
The Finnish would find it difficult if Sweden and Denmark stayed out for a long time and Spain equally so if Italy was out because trade flows between the two are significant.
"I guess that if we make it to EMU, if Germany and France make it, then the Benelux countries, Austria, Ireland will be in as well as Finland, Portugal and Spain.
Italy would not be able to join if it did not pursue policies demonstrating a sustainable path to fiscal deficits in the vicinity of three percent of GDP or below.

To achieve that Italy needs to reform its pension system, he said. "If they don't achieve that now I believe that none of the recommendations, either by the commission or the European Monetary Institute in their reports at the end of this year will support Italian participation."
But he said he expected the Italian government would fight hard and probably approve pension reform, thus opening the way for inclusion.
He said that if the euro comes into existence it will be a strong currency, driven by the constitution of the European Central Bank and its probable policies.

The ECB was second to none in terms of quality for an institution oriented toards price stability. "There is only one target for European monetary policy. It is price stability. There is a clear ruling out of financing any government and international institution deficit through the printing press."
But initially the strength of the euro will be slowed by low growth in Europe and thus the ECB will not need to raise interest rates.
